Swift Syntax: Swift uses `var` for mutable variables, `let` for constants. No semicolons needed. Parentheses around conditions are optional. Braces are required for all control flow.
Basic Types: Swift's fundamental types: Int, Double, Float, Bool, String, Character. Collection types: Array, Set, Dictionary. All types are strongly inferred and strictly checked at compile time.

let pi: Double = 3.14159
var count: Int = 42
let done = false
let items: [Int] = [1, 2, 3]
print("\(pi) \(count) \(done) \(items)")
Variables & Constants: `let` declares constants (immutable binding). `var` declares variables (mutable). Type inference is common, but types can be annotated explicitly. Swift is type-safe with no implicit conversions.

let maxItems = 100
var counter = 0
var name: String = "Alice"
var isActive = true
print("\(name), \(counter), \(isActive)")
What is Swift: Swift is Apple's modern programming language for iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, and beyond. It combines the performance of compiled languages with the expressiveness of scripting languages. Open-sourced in 2015.
Xcode & Playgrounds: Xcode is the official IDE for Swift development. Playgrounds provide interactive coding environments with live results, timeline views, and inline visualization of values.
Swift Versions: Swift evolves rapidly. Swift 5.9 introduced macros and parameter packs. Swift 5.10 completed actor isolation. Swift 6 enhances concurrency safety and enables strict concurrency checking by default.

#if swift(>=5.9)
print("Using Swift 5.9+")
#else
print("Older Swift version")
#endif
Swift REPL & Format: Swift has an interactive REPL (Read-Eval-Print-Loop) for quick experimentation. `swift format` auto-formats code. `swiftc` compiles directly. Run with `swift` in terminal.

Variables & Types.exp: Variables and data types in Swift.

Lists & Navigation: `List` renders scrollable rows. `NavigationStack` enables push navigation. `NavigationLink` links to detail views. Use `\.self` for identifiable data or custom Identifiable conformance.
View Protocol: SwiftUI views conform to the `View` protocol. The `body` computed property describes the view hierarchy. Views are lightweight value types describing UI.
Modifiers: Modifiers configure views. Each modifier returns a new view. Order matters. Common modifiers: .padding(), .font(), .foregroundColor(), .frame(), .background(), .clipShape(), .shadow().
@State: `@State` creates mutable state within a view. SwiftUI automatically updates the view when state changes. Use `private` access. State is owned by the view's storage.
@Binding: `@Binding` creates a two-way connection to a source of truth owned by a parent view. Use `$` prefix to pass binding. Child views read/write through the binding.
@Observable: SwiftUI 6+ uses `@Observable` macro for observable objects (replacing `ObservableObject`). SwiftUI tracks property reads and only updates views when observed properties change.
@Environment: `@Environment` reads values from the view's environment. System environments: colorScheme, locale, managedObjectContext, dismiss. Custom environments via `.environment()` modifier.
StateObject & ObservedObject: `@StateObject` creates and owns a reference-type observable object. `@ObservedObject` observes an object owned elsewhere. `@StateObject` ensures the object lives across view recreation.
State Management Deep: @State (local), @Binding (passed), @ObservedObject (reference type), @StateObject (owned reference), @EnvironmentObject (injected), @AppStorage (UserDefaults), @SceneStorage (scene state). @Published in ObservableObject triggers view updates. Observable macro (iOS 17+) simplifies observation with @Observable class. Use @Environment for system settings (colorScheme, locale, dismiss).

Numeric Types: Swift offers Int (signed), UInt (unsigned), Int8/16/32/64, Float (32-bit), Double (64-bit), and CGFloat. Use `.random(in:)` for randomization. Overflow trapping prevents silent truncation.

let a: Int8 = 100
let b: UInt = 42
let pi: Float = 3.14159
let precise: Double = 3.14159265358979
let dice = Int.random(in: 1...6)
let masked = a &+ 50  // overflow addition &+
print(dice)
Tuples: Tuples group multiple values into a single compound value. Values can be accessed by position (.0, .1) or by name. Tuples are value types useful for returning multiple values.
Type Inference: Swift infers types from literal values and expressions. The compiler deduces the type without explicit annotations. Inference works across function returns, closures, and complex expressions.

let pi = 3.14159        // inferred as Double
let count = 42          // inferred as Int
let message = "Hello"  // inferred as String
let result = count * 2  // inferred as Int
print(type(of: pi))      // Double
Type Safety: Swift is a type-safe language. Every value has a known type at compile time. Type mismatches produce compiler errors, preventing runtime type errors. No implicit type conversions.

let value: Int = 42
// let invalid: String = value  // ERROR: cannot convert
let converted = String(value)   // explicit conversion
print(converted)
Type Aliases: `typealias` creates an alternative name for an existing type. Improves code readability and abstracts complex types like closures or generic types.
Booleans & Characters: Bool has `true` and `false`. Character is a single Unicode grapheme cluster. `String` is a collection of Characters. Use toggle() to flip a Bool value.

var isOn = true
isOn.toggle()
print(isOn)  // false

let star: Character = "⭐️"
let chars: [Character] = ["H", "e", "l", "l", "o"]
print(String(chars))
Any & AnyObject: `Any` can represent any type (including functions and optionals). `AnyObject` represents any class instance. Avoid using these in favor of generics and protocol types for type safety.

if / else: `if` and `else` work as expected. Conditions must be Bool expressions (no truthiness). Swift supports `if let` for optional binding and `if case` for pattern matching.
switch: `switch` supports pattern matching, ranges, tuples, value binding, and where clauses. No implicit fallthrough — use `fallthrough` explicitly. Must be exhaustive with `default` or all cases covered.

let value = 3
switch value {
case 1:
    print("one")
case 2...5:
    print("two to five")
case let n where n % 2 == 0:
    print("even")
default:
    print("other")
}
for-in & while: `for-in` iterates over sequences, ranges, and collections. `while` loops on a condition. `repeat-while` guarantees at least one execution. Use `break` and `continue` for flow control.
if case & guard let: `if case` pattern-matches without a full switch. `guard let` unwraps optionals with early exit, reducing nested `if-let` blocks. `guard` must transfer control (return, break, throw).
for where: `for where` filters loop iterations inline. Combines iteration with condition without nesting an `if` inside the loop body.
Labeled Statements: Labels identify loops and switch statements for precise `break` and `continue` control. Useful for breaking out of nested loops.
Availability Check: `#available` checks API availability at runtime. `@available` marks declarations with minimum platform versions. Guard against using unavailable APIs on older OS versions.
#warning & #error: `#warning` emits a compiler warning. `#error` emits a compiler error, preventing compilation. Useful for TODOs, reminders, and blocking incomplete code from shipping.

Operator Functions: Custom types can implement operators as static functions. Precedence groups define evaluation order. Define both prefix/postfix/infix and assignment variants.
Function Declaration: Functions use `func` keyword. Parameters have argument labels (external) and parameter names (internal). `_` omits the external label. Return type with `->`. Functions are first-class types.
Nested Functions: Functions can be defined inside other functions. Nested functions capture variables from the enclosing scope (closures). Useful for helper logic that is only relevant within a single function.
inout Parameters: `inout` parameters allow functions to modify variables passed as arguments. Use `&` prefix when calling. The parameter is copied-in, modified, and copied-out (copy-in copy-out).

func swapValues(_ a: inout Int, _ b: inout Int) {
    let temp = a
    a = b
    b = temp
}

var x = 10
var y = 20
swapValues(&x, &y)
print(x, y)  // 20, 10
@discardableResult: `@discardableResult` suppresses the unused-result compiler warning. Use when a function performs work through side effects and the result is optional to consume.
Variadic Parameters: Variadic parameters accept zero or more values of the same type. Use `...` after the type. Inside the function, the parameter is an array. Only one variadic per function.
Closures: Closures are anonymous function literals. Syntax: `{ (params) -> ReturnType in body }`. Trailing closure syntax omits parameter labels. Shorthand: `$0`, `$1`. Closures capture surrounding context.
autoclosure: `@autoclosure` wraps an expression in a closure automatically, delaying evaluation until called. Useful for short-circuiting, lazy evaluation, and assertion-style APIs.

Arrays: Ordered, zero-indexed collections. Type-safe and grow dynamically. Methods: append, insert, remove, map, filter, reduce, sort, forEach, first, last.

var items = [1, 2, 3]
items.append(4)
items.insert(0, at: 0)
let doubled = items.map { $0 * 2 }
let evens = items.filter { $0 % 2 == 0 }
print(items)
print(doubled)
print(evens)
Sets: Unordered collections of unique values. `Set<Element>`. Efficient membership testing with `contains`. Set operations: union, intersection, subtracting, symmetricDifference.

let a: Set = [1, 2, 3, 4]
let b: Set = [3, 4, 5, 6]
print(a.union(b).sorted())
print(a.intersection(b).sorted())
print(a.subtracting(b).sorted())
print(a.contains(3))
Lazy Sequences: `lazy` defers computation until elements are accessed. Avoids creating intermediate arrays. Chain multiple transformations efficiently with lazy evaluation.
zip & sequence: `zip(_:_:)` pairs elements from two sequences into tuples (stops at shortest). `sequence(first:next:)` and `sequence(state:next:)` generate infinite/lazy sequences.
Dictionaries: Key-value collections with hashable keys. `[Key: Value]`. Access and modify with subscript. `updateValue(_:forKey:)` returns optional old value. Use `default` subscript for safe access.

var scores: [String: Int] = [:]
scores["Alice"] = 100
scores["Bob"] = 85
scores["Alice"] = 95
for (name, score) in scores {
    print("\(name): \(score)")
}
print(scores["Charlie", default: 0])
Slice: Array slices are lightweight views into portions of an array. They share memory with the original. Use Array(slice) to create a new array. Preserves indices of the original.

let numbers = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
let slice = numbers[1...3]
print(slice)           // [1, 2, 3]
print(slice.startIndex) // 1
print(Array(slice))    // [1, 2, 3]

let prefix = numbers.prefix(3)
let suffix = numbers.suffix(2)
print(Array(prefix))   // [0, 1, 2]
anySatisfy & allSatisfy: `allSatisfy` checks if every element meets a condition. `contains(where:)` checks if any element matches. `first(where:)` finds the first match.

let numbers = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
print(numbers.allSatisfy { $0.isMultiple(of: 2) })  // true
print(numbers.contains { $0 > 5 })                   // true
print(numbers.first { $0 > 5 } ?? 0)                 // 6
print(numbers.firstIndex { $0 == 6 } ?? -1)          // 2
reduce into: `reduce(into:)` accumulates into a mutable result (usually a collection). More efficient than `reduce` for building arrays/dictionaries since it avoids copying.

let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
let grouped = numbers.reduce(into: [String: [Int]]()) { dict, n in
    let key = n.isMultiple(of: 2) ? "even" : "odd"
    dict[key, default: []].append(n)
}
print(grouped)

let squares = numbers.reduce(into: [Int]()) { $0.append($1 * $1) }

Optional Basics: Optionals represent values that may be nil. `Type?` is syntactic sugar for `Optional<T>`. Unwrap with `!` (force), `if let`, `guard let`, or nil-coalescing `??`.
map & flatMap on Optionals: Optionals conform to map/flatMap. `map` transforms an optional's value if non-nil, preserving nil. `flatMap` flattens nested optionals. Chains transformations without unwrapping.
Optional Chaining: Optional chaining (`?.`) safely accesses properties and methods on optional values. Returns nil if any link in the chain is nil. Can be chained multiple levels deep.
Implicitly Unwrapped Optionals: IUOs (`Type!`) automatically force-unwrap when accessed. Used for properties that start nil but are set before use (e.g., IBOutlets). Safer to use regular optionals in new code.
Nil Coalescing Deep: `??` unwraps an optional with a default value. `??` can chain multiple fallbacks. Combine with ternary and `?:` for concise optional handling.

let name: String? = nil
let nickname: String? = nil
let display = name ?? nickname ?? "Guest"
print(display)  // Guest

let values: [Int?] = [nil, 1, nil, 2]
let flat = values.compactMap { $0 }
print(flat)  // [1, 2]
Optional Pattern Matching: Optionals integrate with switch-case pattern matching. Match `.some` and `.none` directly, or use optional pattern `let x?`. Works with `if case` and `for case`.
Optional Chaining Deep: Optional chaining (`?.`) short-circuits if nil. Can chain multiple levels: `person?.address?.city`. Returns optional at each level. Use `!` only when guaranteed non-nil. `??` nil-coalescing provides default. Combine with map/flatMap on optionals for functional transformations. Multiple optional binding: `if let a = x, let b = y { }`. Optional pattern matching in switch.

Mutating Methods: Value types cannot modify their properties in methods by default. Mark methods `mutating` to allow self-modification. Mutating methods can reassign self entirely.
Structs Deep: Structs are value types. They receive automatic memberwise initializers. Properties can have observers (willSet, didSet). Mutating methods can modify self. Copy on write for performance.
Classes Deep: Classes are reference types. Support inheritance, deinitializers, and multiple references to the same instance. ARC manages memory. Use `===` for identity comparison.
Properties & Observers: Stored properties hold values. Computed properties calculate on access. Property observers willSet/didSet watch changes. lazy properties initialize on first access.
Static Subscript: Types can have static subscripts, enabling type-level subscript access. Useful for registry patterns, default values, and lookup tables.
Subclass Deep: Classes support single inheritance. Override methods with `override` keyword. `final` prevents overriding. `super` accesses parent. `required` init ensures subclasses implement it.
Convenience & Required Init: `convenience init` calls another init (delegating). `required init` forces subclasses to implement it. `failable init?` returns nil. `designated init` is the primary initializer.
@objc & Dynamic: `@objc` exposes Swift declarations to Objective-C runtime. Required for target-action patterns, KVO, and some UIKit APIs. `dynamic` enables method swizzling via ObjC dispatch.

Associated Types Deep: Associated types (`associatedtype`) define placeholder types within protocols. Concrete types are resolved by the conforming type. Use `where` clauses for additional constraints.
Opaque Types: `some` keyword hides the concrete return type while preserving protocol conformance. The compiler knows the concrete type. Enables abstraction without generics at the call site.
Existential Types: `any` keyword creates an existential box for protocol types. Unlike `some` (opaque), `any` can hold any conforming type at runtime with a performance cost of the existential container.
Conditional Conformance: Types can conform to protocols only under certain conditions using `extension: where`. Enables powerful composability like Array: Equatable only when Element: Equatable.
Protocols: Protocols define blueprints of methods, properties, and requirements. Structs, classes, and enums can adopt protocols. Protocols can have default implementations via extensions.
Extensions: Extensions add functionality to existing types. Add computed properties, methods, initializers, subscripts, and protocol conformance. Cannot override existing or add stored properties.
Protocol Composition: Protocol composition combines multiple protocols into a single requirement using `&`. A type must conform to all composed protocols. Use with type annotations and generic constraints.
Default Implementations: Protocol extensions provide default method implementations. Conforming types can override or use the default. Combine with constrained extensions for conditional defaults.

Enum Basics: Enums define a common type for a group of related values. Can have methods, computed properties, and initializers. Cases are first-class values.
Associated Values: Enum cases can carry associated values of any type. Each case can have different associated types. Enables tagged unions and the Result pattern.
Indirect Enums: `indirect` enables recursive enums where a case references the enum itself. Required for recursive data structures like lists and trees. Mark individual cases or the whole enum.
CaseIterable: `CaseIterable` protocol auto-generates an array of all enum cases. Access via `AllCases`. Works for enums without associated values. Useful for menus, pickers, and iteration.
@unknown default: `@unknown default` handles future enum cases without breaking exhaustive switches. The compiler warns if all known cases are not covered. Use alongside explicit cases.
Raw Values: Enums can have raw values of String, Character, Int, or floating-point types. Raw values are unique per case. Auto-increment for Int if unspecified. Access with `.rawValue`.

Generic Types: Generic types like `Array<T>` work with any element type. Define custom generic structs, classes, and enums with type parameters. Methods can add their own generic parameters.
Phantom Types: Phantom types are generic parameters not used in the struct's stored properties. They add type-level state without runtime overhead. Enforce invariants at compile time.
Generic Functions: Generic functions work with any type. Type parameters (`<T>`) represent placeholders. Type constraints (`where T: Equatable`) restrict allowed types. Swift infers type parameters at call sites.
Generic Where Clauses: `where` clauses add constraints to generic parameters and associated types. Specify conformance, inheritance, and equality relationships between types.
Constrained Extensions: Extensions on generic types can be constrained with `where` clauses. Methods and properties inside constrained extensions are only available when the constraints are met.
Type Erasure: Type erasure wraps a concrete generic type into an abstract type, hiding the generic parameter. Common patterns: AnySequence, AnyPublisher. Implement via a box/wrapper class.
some & any Keywords: `some` (opaque types, Swift 5.1) hides the concrete return type: `some View`. The compiler knows the concrete type; caller doesn't. `any` (existential types, Swift 5.6) erases the concrete type: `any Equatable`. Caller can store heterogeneous values. `some` enables efficient polymorphism (no box); `any` has runtime overhead from existential containers. Opaque types preserve identity; existentials don't.

POP Principles: Protocol-Oriented Programming is a core Swift paradigm (from The Swift Programming Language): start with a protocol, provide default implementations via extensions, use protocol inheritance and composition. Prefer protocols over superclasses for flexibility.
Protocol Inheritance & Composition: Protocols can inherit from multiple protocols (unlike classes). Protocol composition `&` combines requirements. Use `AnyObject` protocol for class-only protocols. From The Swift Programming Language.
Protocol Extensions & Defaults: Protocol extensions provide default implementations, computed properties, and methods. Constrained extensions (`where`) add capabilities only when specific conditions are met. This powers Swift's standard library.
Empty Protocols (Marker): Empty protocols mark types with a semantic property without requiring methods. `Sendable`, `Codable`, `Hashable` are examples. Combined with constrained extensions and generics.
Self Requirements: Protocols can use `Self` to reference the conforming type. `Equatable` uses Self for ==. `Identifiable` uses Self for ID. Useful for type-safe comparison, copying, and factory patterns.

Access Control: Swift's access levels: `open` (subclassable outside module), `public` (visible outside module), `internal` (default, module-wide), `fileprivate` (file scope), `private` (declaration scope). Use the most restrictive level possible.
Custom ViewModifier & Animation: Custom `ViewModifier` encapsulates reusable view styling. Combine with `withAnimation` for animated transitions. From Hacking with Swift's practical SwiftUI patterns.
Date & Time Handling: Swift provides `Date`, `DateFormatter`, `Calendar`, `DateComponents`, and `DateInterval`. Use `RelativeDateTimeFormatter` for human-readable relative dates. From Hacking with Swift.
SwiftUI Preferences & Custom Layout: Preferences pass data from child to parent views in SwiftUI. `PreferenceKey` aggregates values. `GeometryReader` for layout calculations. From Hacking with Swift's advanced SwiftUI coverage.
UIKit Integration with SwiftUI: SwiftUI can wrap UIKit views via `UIViewRepresentable` and `UIViewControllerRepresentable`. Bridge UIKit delegates, data sources, and target-action patterns. From Hacking with Swift.
URLSession & Networking: Swift's URLSession provides async HTTP networking. `data(from:)` for GET requests, `upload(for:from:)` for POST. Combine with Codable for type-safe JSON parsing. From Hacking with Swift.

do / try / catch: Errors are thrown with `throw` from `Error` conforming types. `try` calls throwing functions. `do/catch` handles errors. Catch specific cases before generic. `defer` runs cleanup on scope exit.
try? & try! Deep: `try?` converts throwing expressions to optional (nil on error). `try!` disables error propagation, crashing on failure. Use `try?` for optional handling, `try!` only when guaranteed.
Result Type: `Result<Success, Failure>` captures either a success value or error as a value. Useful for async callbacks, composeable error handling, and mapping over errors.
Throwing Properties: Properties can throw errors by delegating to throwing functions in their getter. Computed properties marked with `get throws` (Swift 5.9+).
Throwing Subscripts: Subscripts can throw errors (Swift 5.9+). Access elements with `try` when the subscript can fail. Useful for safe collection access beyond bounds.
rethrowing: `rethrows` indicates a function only throws if its closure parameter throws. The function itself never throws directly. Enables higher-order functions that preserve throw behavior.
Defer: `defer` schedules code to execute when the current scope exits, regardless of errors or early returns. Multiple defers execute in reverse order (stack-like).
Custom Errors: Custom error types conform to the `Error` protocol (or `Swift.LocalizedError`). Use enums with associated values for structured error information.

Input/Output.exp: Input and output operations in Swift.

Binary Targets: Binary targets distribute pre-compiled frameworks (e.g., Firebase, Sentry). Reference remote .xcframework URLs or local paths. SPM downloads and links the binary.
SPM Plugins: Swift Package Manager plugins extend build processes. Build Tool Plugins run before compilation (code gen, linting). Command Plugins run on-demand (formatting, documentation).
Macro Targets: Swift macros generate code at compile time. SPM 5.9+ supports macro targets. Macros reduce boilerplate and can introspect code at compile time.
SPM Commands: Key SPM commands: `swift build`, `swift test`, `swift run`, `swift package generate-xcodeproj`, `swift package --version`. Resolution info with `swift package show-dependencies`.

# Terminal commands:
# swift build              # Build package
# swift test               # Run tests
# swift run <target>       # Run executable
# swift package clean      # Clean build artifacts
# swift package resolve    # Resolve dependencies
# swift package show-dependencies  # Show dependency tree
# swift package plugin --list     # List available plugins
Creating Libraries: Create reusable Swift packages: `swift package init --type library`. Package.swift defines targets, dependencies, products. Mark API with `public` access control. Document with `///` doc comments. Version with semantic versioning. Publish on GitHub and add via SPM URL. Use `@available` for platform version gating.
Package.swift: SPM uses Package.swift manifest. Define targets, dependencies, products in a declarative Swift DSL. `// swift-tools-version: 5.9` declares the manifest version.
Package Structure: Standard SPM layout: Sources/PackageName/*.swift, Tests/PackageNameTests/*.swift, Package.swift at root. Resources in Sources/PackageName/Resources/. Use `.target(name:resources:)` to declare.

MyPackage/
└── Package.swift
└── Sources/
│   └── MyPackage/
│       └── Core.swift
│       └── Resources/
│           └── data.json
└── Tests/
    └── MyPackageTests/
        └── CoreTests.swift
Build Settings: SPM supports Swift compiler flags, linker flags, C settings, and preprocessor macros per target and configuration. Conditionally apply with `.when(platforms:, configuration:)`.

ARC Deep: Automatic Reference Counting manages memory for class instances. Each strong reference increments the count. Deallocation happens at zero. `deinit` for cleanup. Retain cycles prevent deallocation.
Strong Reference Cycles: Strong reference cycles (retain cycles) occur when two instances hold strong references to each other. Memory is never reclaimed. Use `weak` or `unowned` to break cycles.
unowned vs weak Deep: `weak` references auto-nil when object deallocates, always optional. `unowned` assumes object lives at least as long, non-optional (crash on access after dealloc). Use weak for optional relationship, unowned for guaranteed co-lifetime.
@NSCopying: `@NSCopying` copies the property value on assignment using the NSCopying protocol. Ensures the instance holds its own copy rather than sharing mutable reference.
ARC & Reference Cycles: Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) manages memory for reference types (classes). Each strong reference increments count; deinit occurs when count reaches 0. Strong reference cycles: class A holds strong ref to B, B holds strong ref to A. Break with `weak` (optional, auto-nilled on dealloc) or `unowned` (non-optional, crash if accessed after dealloc). Closures capture self strongly — use [weak self] or [unowned self].
Closure Capture Lists: Closures capture references strongly by default. Capture lists `[weak self]` or `[unowned self]` break retain cycles with closures. Use weak for escaping closures to avoid cycles.
Memory Layout: `MemoryLayout` provides the size, alignment, and stride of any type. Useful for understanding struct packing, interop with C, and performance optimization.

struct Point {
    var x: Double
    var y: Double
}

print(MemoryLayout<Int>.size)         // 8
print(MemoryLayout<Int>.stride)       // 8
print(MemoryLayout<Int>.alignment)    // 8

print(MemoryLayout<Point>.size)       // 16
print(MemoryLayout<Point>.stride)     // 16

print(MemoryLayout<Bool>.size)        // 1
print(MemoryLayout<Bool>.stride)      // 1

print(MemoryLayout<Int?>.size)        // 9 (Optional enum with associated)

Opaque Parameter Types: Swift 5.7+ allows `some` in function parameter position (like `some View`). Equivalent to a generic parameter with a protocol constraint but written more concisely.
KeyPaths: Key paths (`\Type.property`) provide type-safe references to properties. `WritableKeyPath` for mutable access. Useful for functional programming, sorting, and binding.
Dynamic Member Lookup: `@dynamicMemberLookup` enables dot-syntax access to arbitrary properties via a `subscript(dynamicMember:)` method. Useful for JSON handling, scripting, and DSLs.
@propertyWrapper Deep: Property wrappers encapsulate getter/setter logic. Custom wrappers use `@propertyWrapper` with `wrappedValue`. `projectedValue` provides additional API via `$` prefix.
Codable & JSON Deep: `Codable` (Encodable & Decodable) auto-generates serialization. Custom keys with `CodingKeys` enum. Custom encoding/decoding via `encode(to:)` and `init(from:)`.
Regex: Swift 5.7+ introduces native regex literals `/pattern/`. `Regex<Output>` type with type-safe captures. Use `firstMatch`, `wholeMatch`, and `matches` for matching.
Opaque vs Existential: `some` (opaque) preserves concrete type identity at compile time. `any` (existential) boxes the type at runtime. Some types work for return values; any types work for heterogeneous collections.
Macros (Swift 5.9+): Swift macros (Swift 5.9+) generate code at compile time. Freestanding macros (#stringify, #warning). Attached macros (@Observable, @Test, @MainActor). Declared with `@macro` or via external module. Built-in: #Preview, #Predicate. Macro roles: @freestanding(expression), @freestanding(declaration), @attached(member), @attached(conformance), @attached(peer).
Result Builders: Result builders (formerly function builders) construct complex values from a block of statements. Power SwiftUI's DSL, AttributedStringBuilder, and custom DSLs.

AsyncSequence Deep: AsyncSequence provides asynchronous iteration over values over time. `AsyncStream` creates custom async sequences. `AsyncAlgorithms` package adds zip, merge, combineLatest.
Actors Deep: Actors protect mutable state with actor isolation. Only one task accesses actor state at a time. `nonisolated` for methods that don't access actor state. `isolated` parameters for cross-actor calls.
Task Groups: Task groups create structured concurrency trees. Tasks added run in parallel. Group collects all results before returning. `withThrowingTaskGroup` for throwing tasks.
MainActor: `@MainActor` ensures code runs on the main actor (main thread). Mark types, functions, or closures. `await` required when calling from non-main context.
Global Actors: Global actors provide shared concurrency isolation across types. Define with `@globalActor`. All properties/methods of an actor-isolated type share the same executor.
Sendable: `Sendable` protocol guarantees a type is safe to share across concurrency domains. Value types are implicitly Sendable. Classes must be final with immutable state or use actor isolation.
Task Local Values: Task-local values propagate through the async task hierarchy. Scoped to specific task trees. Useful for logging context, request IDs, and configuration that follows async flow.
async/await: Swift's structured concurrency uses async functions and await calls. async functions can suspend and resume, freeing the thread. Building block for all modern Swift concurrency.
async let: `async let` launches a child task that runs concurrently with the current task. All async let bindings must be awaited before the enclosing scope exits.
